title: Mandaviya Joins Indian Diaspora Cycle Ride to Cheer Asian Games Athletes
excerpt: Union Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya cycled alongside members of the Indian community in Nagoya on Sunday as the diaspora rallied behind India's 500-strong contingent at the 20th Asian Games.
body:
• Union Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya joined members of the Indian diaspora in Nagoya, Japan, for a special 'Sundays on Cycle' event organised to cheer India's athletes at the Asian Games.
  • Mandaviya said the diaspora had made "all the arrangements" to encourage the contingent, with many young Indian volunteers supporting the team in Nagoya.
  • The 20th Asian Games opened on Saturday at the Paloma Mizuho Stadium, with double Olympic medallist Manu Bhaker and kabaddi star Pawan Sehrawat carrying India's flag.
  • India's contingent of just over 500 athletes is competing across 36 sports at the continental meet, which runs from September 19 to October 4.

Union Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya spent Sunday morning cycling alongside members of the Indian diaspora in Nagoya, joining a special 'Sundays on Cycle' event organised by the Indian community in Japan to cheer on the country's athletes at the 20th Asian Games.

Speaking to the IANS news agency on the sidelines of the Games, Mandaviya praised the diaspora for rallying behind the contingent. "The Asian Games have started in Nagoya, Japan, and 503 youths from India have come to participate in the Games. Today, India's Diaspora has organised a Sunday on Cycling event in Nagoya. I am happy that our contingent is performing well, and our Diaspora is encouraging them," he said.

Diaspora as the twelfth man

Mandaviya framed the community's role as part of a larger pattern of diaspora support for India. "Naturally, the Diaspora is a strength in our country. Wherever the Indian people are in need, our Diaspora is always there to support them. In Nagoya, the Diaspora has made all the arrangements to encourage our Indian athletes. Many youths are working as volunteers. This is the specialty of India," he told IANS.

Speaking separately to ANI, the minister expressed confidence that India's athletes would perform strongly and bring glory and pride to the nation. The cycling event brought together Indian volunteers and community members just as the Games' sporting programme gathered pace, with the diaspora positioning itself as both cheerleader and logistical backbone for the visiting contingent.

"Naturally, the Diaspora is a strength in our country. Wherever the Indian people are in need, our Diaspora is always there to support them."

— Mansukh Mandaviya, Union Sports Minister

The Games begin

The 20th Asian Games were formally opened on Saturday evening with a ceremony at the Paloma Mizuho Stadium in Nagoya. Double Olympic medallist Manu Bhaker — who won two bronze medals in shooting at the Paris 2024 Olympics — and kabaddi star Pawan Sehrawat led the Indian contingent as flagbearers. Sehrawat, a member of India's gold-medal-winning men's kabaddi team at the previous Asian Games, was named the male flagbearer in place of shot-putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor following technical issues, ANI reported.

India is represented by a contingent of just over 500 athletes — Mandaviya put the number at 503, while agency reports listed 501 athletes competing across 36 sports — at a Games bringing together athletes from 45 countries and regions across 43 sports and 469 medal events, running through October 4.

What to watch

Sunday's programme carried a heavy Indian presence: the cricket teams began their campaigns, teqball star Quimcy Dsouza chased a medal, and shooters including Elavenil Valarivan were in action. The swimming finals, athletics programme and the defence of India's kabaddi titles will shape the coming week.

For the Indian community in Japan — one of the smaller but fast-growing diaspora populations in East Asia — the Nagoya Games are a rare chance to support the national team on home turf. If Sunday's cycle ride is any indication, the athletes will not lack for familiar voices in the stands.
